title: Horizontal vs vertical scaling

options.t: Adding more CPU and RAM to one server
Adding more server instances and distributing load across them

explanation: Horizontal scaling improves availability and has no single-machine ceiling, but needs load balancing and stateless or shared-state services.

title: Stateless services
body: Why do stateless application servers make horizontal scaling easier?

options.t: Any instance can handle any request, so load balancers can route freely and instances can be added or removed safely

explanation: Move session/state to a shared store (Redis, database) or into signed tokens. Sticky sessions are a workaround that hurts balancing and failover.

title: Cache-aside
body: In the cache-aside pattern, what happens on a cache miss?

options.t: The cache loads data from the database by itself
The application reads from the database, then writes the result into the cache
The database pushes data to the cache

answer: The application loads from the source and populates the cache.
explanation: On writes, update the database then invalidate (delete) the cache entry. Combine with TTLs to bound staleness.

title: Write-through caching

options.t: Writes go only to the cache and are flushed later
Each write updates the cache and the backing store synchronously

answer: Synchronous writes to both cache and store.
explanation: Write-through keeps the cache fresh at the cost of write latency; write-behind is faster but risks data loss if the cache fails before flushing.

title: Cache stampede
body: A hot cache key expires and thousands of concurrent requests hit the database at once. Which mitigation helps most directly?

options.t: Request coalescing / single-flight locking so one request rebuilds the value while others wait or serve stale data

answer: Coalesce rebuilds (and/or serve stale while revalidating, add TTL jitter).
explanation: Other tools: probabilistic early expiration, background refresh of hot keys, and jittered TTLs to avoid synchronised expirations.

title: CAP theorem
body: According to the CAP theorem, what must a distributed data store choose during a network partition?
explanation: Partitions are unavoidable, so the real choice is CP (refuse some requests to stay consistent) or AP (answer with possibly stale data). PACELC adds the latency/consistency trade-off when there is no partition.

title: Sharding hotspots
body: What is a common risk of sharding data by a monotonically increasing key such as a timestamp?

options.t: All new writes land on the same shard, creating a hotspot

answer: Write hotspots on the newest shard.
explanation: Prefer hashed keys or composite keys (tenant + time) for even distribution; use range sharding only when range scans dominate and load is known.

title: Read replicas
body: A user updates their profile and immediately reloads it from a read replica, seeing old data. Why?

options.t: Asynchronous replication lag: the replica has not applied the write yet

explanation: Provide read-your-writes consistency by routing a user's reads to the primary for a short window after writes, or by tracking replication position.

title: At-least-once delivery
body: A message queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. What must consumers do?

options.t: Be idempotent, because the same message may be delivered more than once

explanation: Deduplicate with message ids stored alongside the effect (or idempotent upserts). Use dead-letter queues for poison messages and the outbox pattern to publish reliably with database changes.

title: Circuit breaker
body: What does the circuit breaker pattern do?

options.t: Stops calling a failing dependency for a period after repeated failures, failing fast and allowing it to recover

answer: Fail fast after repeated failures, then probe (half-open).
explanation: States: closed → open (fail fast) → half-open (trial calls). Combine with timeouts, retries with exponential backoff + jitter, and fallbacks.

title: Token bucket rate limiting
body: How does a token bucket rate limiter work?

options.t: It rejects every request after the first
Tokens are added at a fixed rate up to a capacity; each request consumes a token, so short bursts are allowed while the average rate is capped
It counts requests per day only

answer: Refill at rate r, burst up to capacity b.
explanation: Return HTTP 429 with Retry-After when empty. In a distributed system keep counters in a shared store (e.g. Redis) or enforce limits at the API gateway.

title: Consistent hashing
body: Why is consistent hashing used for distributing keys across cache nodes?

options.t: When a node is added or removed only about 1/n of keys move, instead of almost all keys with hash mod n

answer: Minimal key remapping on membership changes.
explanation: Virtual nodes smooth the distribution across physical servers. Used by Dynamo-style stores, distributed caches and load balancers.

title: Design a URL shortener
body: Design a URL shortener handling 100M new links per month and 10:1 read/write ratio. Cover the API, ID generation, storage, caching and scaling.
answer: POST /links returns a short code; GET /{code} redirects (301/302). Generate base62 codes from a distributed ID or random 7-char codes with collision checks, store in a key-value store, cache hot codes, and scale reads with CDN/cache.
explanation:
**Scale:** ~40 writes/s, ~400 reads/s average (plan for 10× peaks); 100M × 12 × ~500 bytes ≈ 600 GB/year.
**API:** `POST /api/links {url, customAlias?, expiresAt?}` → `{code}`; `GET /{code}` → 301 (cacheable) or 302 (to count clicks).
**IDs:** base62 of a 64-bit unique id (Snowflake-style or pre-allocated ranges per server) gives 7–8 chars without collisions; random codes need a uniqueness check.
**Storage:** key-value or document store keyed by code (partition by code hash); replicate for availability.
**Caching:** Redis/CDN for hot codes (reads dominate).
**Analytics:** emit click events to a queue and aggregate asynchronously so redirects stay fast.
**Abuse:** rate limiting, malicious URL scanning, expiration.
reference: Estimate load and storage; define create/redirect APIs; generate collision-free short codes (base62 of unique ids or random with checks); store mappings in a partitioned, replicated key-value store; cache hot mappings and use 301/302 deliberately; process analytics asynchronously; add rate limiting, abuse detection and expiry.
